The ends of five flat filter sheets were coated with conductive paint, and a copper mesh electrode was installed along the ends for electrical continuity. Thermocouples were placed between the central layers for temperature measurement and feedback control. Cycle adsorption and desorption were conducted with the layered filter design. For the cycles, desorption temperature and duration were reduced to 75oC and by 50%, respectively. Under these conditions, the material maintained similar working capacity as the pleated filter tests, indicating an improvement in the heating uniformity. CO adsorbed and desorbed from the laminate configuration over 100 cycles 2 Key Learnings The bench unit testing demonstrated the proof-of-concept design of the structured sorbent filters for DAC application with Joule-heated regeneration. Despite optimizing sorbent performance using the laminated configuration, two issues remained: (1) sorbent CO working capacity was lower than the sorbent granules; 2 and (2) cyclic CO capacity fade was still evident. A sample of the as-received sorbent coated filter was 2 tested in the lab screening reactor. The CO capacity over the course of five adsorption/desorption cycles 2 is shown in Figure 20. The average CO capacity over the five cycles is 0.99 mmol/g, which is a 26% 2 reduction in the CO capacity of the sorbent compared to the synthesized, uncoated ECCOSorb-T1 granules. 2 This suggests that the adhesive coating used to bind the sorbent to the filter substrate could block sorbent sites and reduce overall capacity of the material. This is further supported by surface area analysis, which revealed a 30% reduction in surface area of the coated sample. Based on discussions with our commercial partner, it was concluded that the binder used is likely also causing cyclic degradation in the sorbent performance. Future work with commercial partner will focus on optimizing the binder amount and type to minimize sorbent performance loss. Final Technical Report – Unlimited Rights Data 21 Susteon Inc.
